planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Willamette is self-incompatible and needs a compatible pollenizer cultivar with overlapping bloom nearby.

directions: Released by Oregon State University in the mid-1970s, Willamette was for decades the dominant commercial hazelnut in the Willamette Valley before newer blight-resistant releases like Jefferson and Yamhill took over much of the acreage. It bears medium-sized, good-quality nuts on a moderately vigorous, upright tree and ripens in mid-season, ahead of many older varieties. Like most pre-1990s Pacific Northwest cultivars it carries only limited resistance to eastern filbert blight, so orchard sanitation and, where needed, fungicide timing matter more than with modern resistant selections. Plant with a distinct, cross-compatible pollenizer within about 100 feet for reliable nut set.
sources: Oregon State University College of Agricultural Sciences

common_name: Kentish Cob Filbert (Lambert's Filbert, Classic English Cobnut)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in spring; Kentish Cob is only partially self-fertile and crops far better with a distinct pollenizer such as Cosford nearby.

directions: Kentish Cob, also sold as Lambert's Filbert, is one of the oldest and best-known English cobnut cultivars, long grown commercially in Kent for its elongated, sweet-flavored nuts with a fine flavor. The tree produces its dangling yellow male catkins in late winter well before leaf-out, an attractive early-season feature, but the female flowers need pollen from a genetically distinct hazel to set a full crop, so pairing with Cosford or another compatible cultivar significantly improves yield and nut size. Prune to an open, multi-stemmed bush form and remove root suckers regularly to keep the plant manageable. Harvest in early autumn once husks brown and nuts loosen readily from their cases.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in spring; Cosford is a strong, long-shedding pollen source valued as a pollenizer for Kentish Cob and other cultivars, though it also bears a worthwhile crop of its own.

directions: Cosford is a long-cultivated English cultivar prized both for its own oblong, very thin-shelled, sweet-kernelled nuts and for its value as a dependable pollenizer, since its bright yellow catkins shed pollen abundantly over a long bloom window. It is a hardy, reliable grower across a wide range of soils and produces fewer root suckers than many other hazel cultivars, making it easier to keep tidy. Plant it within an orchard or mixed hedgerow alongside Kentish Cob or other named cultivars so its early, generous pollen shed overlaps with their receptive female flowers. Harvest in late September when the thin, light-brown shells loosen from the husk.

common_name: Tonda di Giffoni Hazelnut (Italian PGI Round Hazelnut)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; self-incompatible, so plant with a distinct pollenizer cultivar for a reliable crop.

directions: Tonda di Giffoni is one of Italy's most celebrated hazelnut cultivars, grown around Giffoni in Campania and protected under EU Protected Geographical Indication status for its round, easily-peeled, richly flavored kernels favored by confectioners for roasting and chocolate production. The tree is moderately vigorous, precocious, and notably productive, with good tolerance of both cold winter temperatures and common fungal pressures compared to many other European cultivars. It performs best where summers are warm and dry enough to ripen the crop fully, similar to its native growing region. Harvest from early September into mid-October once husks brown and nuts drop or twist free easily.

common_name: Merveille de Bollwiller Hazelnut (Hall's Giant, Historic European Filbert)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in spring; partially self-fertile but produces best crops with a distinct pollenizer nearby, and leafs out late, which helps it dodge spring frosts.

directions: Selected in Germany in the late eighteenth century and also sold under the name Hall's Giant, this is one of the oldest named hazelnut cultivars still commercially grown, valued for its large, sweet, thin-shelled nuts and for its long-flowering, purple-blushed catkins that make it a useful cross-pollinator for many other cultivars. The tree is late to leaf out in spring, which helps its young growth avoid frost damage, and it is vigorous and reliably productive once established. Because it is only partially self-fertile, plant it alongside a genetically distinct hazel such as a wild hedgerow hazel or another named cultivar for the heaviest nut set. Harvest in early to mid autumn as the husks color and nuts release freely.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or grafted trees in early spring in deep, well-drained soil; partially self-fertile but yields improve with a second cold-hardy walnut cultivar nearby for cross-pollination.

directions: Broadview is a Canadian-selected English walnut valued in cold-winter regions for hardiness well beyond that of typical Carpathian strains, tolerating winter lows reported near -30F once established. It is protandrous, partially self-fertile, and notably precocious, often bearing a light crop within its first few years from planting, though a second distinct cultivar improves nut set. Its mid-to-late leafing habit helps young growth escape damaging late spring frosts, an important trait for northern growers. Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun and give it room to reach the large mature size typical of English walnuts, harvesting nuts in mid-to-late season once hulls begin to split.

common_name: Serbian Gold Quince (Leskovac, Highly Productive Balkan Quince)

planting.note: Plant a container or bare-root tree in spring in full sun; self-fertile and needs no pollinizer.

directions: Serbian Gold, also sold under its original local name Leskovac, is a heavy-cropping Balkan quince cultivar selected in Serbia in the early twentieth century and now widely distributed through European and North American nurseries for its reliability and good resistance to leaf blight compared with many older quince selections. It forms a broad, low-domed small tree with attractive pale pink spring blossom followed by large, aromatic, golden-yellow fruit that ripens in early to mid autumn. The tree is self-fertile and consistently productive on its own, making it a good single-tree choice for a home garden. Grow in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, and harvest once fruit turns fully golden and gives off its characteristic strong quince fragrance; the raw flesh remains firm and astringent and is best cooked into jelly, paste, or preserves.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; self-fertile and needs no pollinizer.

directions: Sultan is a large-fruited Dutch medlar cultivar grown for abundant crops of fruit up to two inches across, larger than many older medlar selections. Like all medlars, the hard, astringent fruit must be bletted — left on the tree through a hard frost or stored in a cool place for several weeks until the flesh softens and browns — before it develops its rich, wine-like flavor suited to jellies, sauces, and eating fresh as a confection. The tree is self-fertile, ornamental, and undemanding, tolerating poor soils better than most tree fruits, though it fruits best in full sun with good air movement. Pick fruit after the first hard frost of autumn and set it aside to blet before use.
